control_name: Multi-Factor Authentication for Access to In-Scope Systems
objective: Reduce the likelihood that a compromised credential alone grants access to in-scope systems, by requiring a second authentication factor on every path into the environment.
description: All human access to in-scope production systems, the identity provider, the cloud management console, and the source code repository requires a second authentication factor. Enforcement is applied centrally at the identity provider through conditional access policy rather than per-application, and applies to employees, contractors, and administrative accounts. Break-glass accounts are excluded from the policy only where technically unavoidable, and are compensated by vaulted credentials and alerted use.
owner_role: IT / Identity and Access Management owner

conditions: The service organization operates systems reachable with user credentials
Security category is in scope (always true for SOC 2)
not_applicable_when: No interactive human authentication path exists into the in-scope boundary; in that case the equivalent objective is met by workload identity controls instead

implementation_guidance: Enforce at the identity provider with conditional access rather than per-application toggles, so coverage is provable from one place.

Enumerate every authentication path first: SSO, direct application logins, VPN, SSH/bastion, cloud console, cloud CLI, API tokens, and vendor-managed admin portals. Uncovered paths are the usual cause of a design deficiency.
Prefer phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2/WebAuthn) for administrative and privileged access.
Document break-glass accounts explicitly, vault the credentials, and alert on any use.
Treat long-lived API tokens as an authentication path requiring its own compensating control, not as out of scope.
design_considerations: Does enforcement cover every authentication path into the boundary, including non-SSO and administrative paths?
Does it cover contractors, service desk accounts, and third-party support access, not only employees?
Are exclusions from the policy enumerated, justified, and compensated?
operating_considerations: Was the policy in force for the entire examination period, or introduced partway through?
Were exclusions added during the period, and were they approved?
Can the organization demonstrate the configuration did not change, or produce configuration history?

evidence_examples.note: Identity provider policy export showing enforcement scope and any exclusions.
Access review record corroborates the user population the policy applies to.
Configuration change history evidencing that the authentication policy held throughout the period.

risks.description: Credential compromise through phishing or reuse grants direct access to production systems and customer data.
An unenforced authentication path becomes an unmonitored bypass around the intended control.

related_controls.note: Access review verifies the population that MFA enforcement applies to.

source_refs.supports: Identity of the criterion this control is intended to help meet.
Design and operating considerations, and the observation that uncovered authentication paths are a frequent deficiency.
Preference for phishing-resistant factors and central conditional-access enforcement.

notes: MFA is not named as a required control by the trust services criteria. CC6.1 states an objective about logical access security measures; MFA is a common and effective way to help meet it, not a mandate. DriftGuard must phrase it that way.
This control is an exemplar of the canonical control structure, not a catalog entry.

evidence_examples extended to EV-CONFIG-001 in the CC6 phase. EV-IAM-001 is point-in-time; the pairing is what supports a Type 2 conclusion, and the foundation phase recorded its absence as a known gap.
